dialogs.title: စကားပြော — A taxi ride to the Shwedagon Pagoda
dialogs.intro: Ani takes a taxi to Shwedagon. Watch the word ဘယ်, which comes up twice with completely different meanings: once as "which", once as "left". What tells them apart is the word that follows.

grammars.title: ⚠️ ဘယ် — "which" and "left" at once
body: One word, two completely different meanings, and both turn up often in a single taxi ride. Luckily the rule is clear: **ဘယ် meaning "left" is almost always followed by ဘက်**, while ဘယ် meaning "which" is followed by a thing, a place, or a marker.
after: So ဘယ်ဘက်မှာ ရပ်ပါ means "stop on the left", while ဘယ်မှာ ရပ်မလဲ means "where shall I stop?". They sound alike, the meanings are far apart, and the only difference is one syllable: ဘက်.
Its opposite, "right", is ညာဘက် (*nya-bèk*) and has no double meaning at all — so if in doubt, point with your hand while you say it. Myanmar taxi drivers are used to it.

grammars.title: Giving directions
body: Commands in Burmese are simply the plain verb plus ပါ. Nothing changes form, and it's ပါ that makes it sound like a request instead of an order being barked.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: တည့်တည့် သွားပါ
ညာဘက် ကွေ့ပါ
ဘယ်ဘက် ကွေ့ပါ
ဒီမှာ ရပ်ပါ
ပြန်လှည့်ပါ

after: ⚠️ ⚠️ Name your destination by **a well-known landmark**, not a street address. Street addresses in Yangon are rarely used in conversation; people name the nearest pagoda, market, bridge, or building. Say ရွှေတိဂုံနားမှာ ("near Shwedagon") and the driver will know where to go.

grammars.title: …တဲ့ — attaching a description to a noun
body: တဲ့ (*dè.*) turns a whole clause into a description of the noun that follows it. English uses "that/who/which" and puts the clause **after** the noun; Burmese puts it **before**.

head: Burmese
Say it
Literal translation
Meaning
rows: ဦးလေး သိတဲ့ လမ်း
ကျွန်မ ဝယ်တဲ့ စာအုပ်
မနေ့က တွေ့တဲ့ လူ

after: ⚠️ For things that haven't happened yet, use မယ့် (*mè.*) instead of တဲ့: မနက်ဖြန် သွားမယ့် နေရာ (the place we'll go to tomorrow). The pair တဲ့/မယ့် matches the pair တယ်/မယ် you already know from unit 8.

grammars.title: Vehicles and getting around
body: For getting on and off a vehicle, use the verbs တက် ("get on") and ဆင်း ("get off"). Vehicles take the classifier စီး.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: တက်တယ် · ဆင်းတယ်
ကားပိတ်တယ်

after: To say what you travel by, use the marker **နဲ့**: ဘတ်စ်ကားနဲ့ သွားတယ် (go by bus). It's the same "with" as in စာအုပ်နဲ့ သင်တယ် from unit 3 — one marker for every means.

blocks.text: A few things about Myanmar traffic worth knowing before you stand at the roadside waiting for a taxi.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three quirks of Myanmar traffic
items: **Cars drive on the right — but the steering wheel is on the right too.** Myanmar switched from driving on the left to the right in 1970, but most of its cars are imported second-hand from Japan with right-hand drive. So bus drivers have to guess when overtaking, and passengers step out straight into the middle of the road. Take care when crossing.
**Motorbikes have been banned in central Yangon** since 2003. It's the only big city in Southeast Asia without a sea of motorbikes — don't expect motorbike taxis as in Bangkok or Jakarta.
**Taxis don't use meters.** The price is always agreed before you get in, and bargaining is a normal part of it. Ask ဘယ်လောက်လဲ before you open the door, not after you sit down.
